content.title: Let's Be Honest: Remote Workers Are Coasting and Everyone Knows It
content.text:
We are all pretending. Every office manager, every team lead, every person who has sat through a video call and watched a colleague's eyes drift to a second screen knows exactly what is going on. Remote work was supposed to be a grand experiment in trust. What it turned into is the longest paid holiday in the history of employment, and nobody has the nerve to say so.

Let's be honest for once. When someone tells you they are more productive at home, what they mean is that nobody can see them. The laundry is running. The dog has been walked twice. The status light has been green for six hours and the actual output is a two-line message sent at 4:55 so it looks like the day ended with a bang. Everyone knows this. Everyone does it. And everyone acts shocked when someone points it out.

The defenders of remote work love to talk about focus and deep work and the tyranny of the open plan office. Fine. So where is all this deep work? Where are the results? If half the workforce suddenly became twice as productive, we would be swimming in finished projects. Instead we have longer timelines, more meetings about meetings, and a generation of employees who think a camera-off call counts as showing up.

And what about the people who actually do go in? The ones who commute, who sit at a desk, who can be found when something breaks? They are carrying the coasters, and they know it. They cover for the person who is mysteriously unreachable every Friday afternoon. They answer the questions that should have been answered by someone who is technically online. They are the ones keeping the lights on while the remote crowd writes blog posts about work-life balance.

Nobody in leadership will admit any of this because admitting it means admitting they lost control. It is easier to publish a glossy policy about flexibility than to say the obvious: a lot of people are being paid full salaries for part-time effort, and the system has no way to tell the difference.

Do you really believe the person with the perfectly curated home office background is grinding through their backlog? Do you honestly think those wellness walks are followed by a burst of brilliance? Come on. We all know what a Tuesday looks like when nobody is watching.

The truth is simple, and it is UNCOMFORTABLE, which is why nobody says it. Remote work is not a productivity revolution. It is a loophole, and the people exploiting it have gotten very good at defending it with words like autonomy and trust. Trust is earned. Autonomy is for people who deliver. And a green dot is not a work product.

Someone had to say it plainly. If you have watched a remote colleague coast while you picked up the slack, share this with your team and tell us in the comments what the worst example you have seen looks like. Let's stop pretending together.

notes: Rage-bait pitting in-office workers against remote workers with anecdote-shaped assertions presented as universal fact, rhetorical questions and a share/comment hook. A correct judge should flag the absence of data or counterpoints and the reliance on 'everyone knows'.
